article.title: We Must Talk about Denuclearizing Israel
article.author: Socialist Forum
article.content: There is a simple action DSA can take to dramatically change the relationship between the United States and the genocidal regime in Israel. Start talking about their nukes. Openly, aggressively. Denounce Israel as a rogue nuclear state. Since Israel began developing its nuclear program in the 1950s, its nuclear capabilities have remained the subject of longstanding secrecy and diplomatic silence. The U.S. government has refused to acknowledge Israeli weapons for a variety of reasons; a big one is that a Presidential determination would trigger the stiff sanctions in Sec. 102(B) of the Arms Export Control Act. By acknowledging and denouncing Israel’s nuclear arsenal, DSA can force political recognition of these weapons and inspire action, such as imposing sanctions on Israel. Furthermore, the non-recognition of Israeli nuclear weapons creates a political asymmetry in which Iranians become the “bad” guys for wanting to deter Israeli nuclear aggression. If Iran wanted to acquire such weapons, it would not be doing so in a vacuum as though a bunch of mavericks had suddenly introduced nuclear weapons into the Middle East for the first time. Israel already possesses them and is obsessed with destroying the Iranian state. In other words, the public logic of the aggression against Iran, which was launched with the atomically thin justification of denying Iran nuclear weapons, depends upon the continued non-recognition of Israel’s own nuclear arsenal. The imperialist line is even more absurd given that at least until the February 2026 U.S. assassination of Ayatollah Khamenei, Iran had a fatwa (a religious ruling) against building such weapons. Moreover, what is known of Israel’s nuclear policy is that it is alone in the world in continuing to contemplate weapons use against its non-nuclear neighbors explicitly. Yet, this is not the half of it. Israel’s nuclear arsenal helps explain several otherwise puzzling aspects of the U.S.-Israel “special relationship.” Why does the genocidal regime in Tel Aviv exercise such extraordinary influence over U.S. policy? Why do countries around the world, despite widespread disgust at Israeli and American genocide and aggression, have been unwilling or unable to forcefully intervene? Why do the weaker nations of the world allow international law to be discarded so casually? What would be needed to stop Israel for good? The Israeli nuclear arsenal is a key under-discussed factor. The U.S. socialist movement, including our elected leaders, is not anywhere near where we need to be in terms of formal influence over public policy around these issues, yet this shouldn’t mean total silence. We have a bully pulpit from which to speak, and we must engage all levers of power to stop the genocidal Israeli grab for lebensraum. U.S. support for Israel cannot simply be explained by some timeless affinity with Jewish people, given the history of U.S. antisemitism. There are sticky factors that are tying American imperialism to this specific colonial outpost, and a big one is the bomb. Nuclear containment with flowers The American state consists of both a rational part and an ideological part. There must be something that is firmly convincing the rational actors to let the ideologues have their way. Israel is a tiny nuclear state with a huge victim complex that is highly militarily vulnerable should its subsidies be cut off. It is unique in that it is the only nuclear state that is not formally acknowledged. A formal admission by the U.S. that Israel is nuclear-armed would trigger domestic sanctions and begin major reorientations in the region. Of all the countries that have acquired nukes after the 1967 Non-Proliferation Treaty cutoff (the DPRK, India, Israel, and Pakistan), Pakistan and the DPRK are subject to sanctions. India was subject to stricter sanctions, but craftily cut a deal with the U.S. in 2008, and more of those sanctions are being removed . Israel alone has avoided sanctions entirely. Apartheid South Africa, a nuclear collaborator with Israel, also attempted this trick, but when the Afrikaner regime finally collapsed, they dismantled their small stockpile of nuclear weapons to avoid letting them fall into the hands of Black Africans. Notwithstanding the occasional slip-up, U.S. politicians do not acknowledge Israel’s nuclear status, and Israeli politicians are usually ( but not always ) oblique about it. This suppresses most official discussion of nuclear policy around Israel, though academics and journalists will sometimes speak up on the margins. Congresspeople do not discuss the issue publicly since it goes against the U.S.’s unofficial but rigid nuclear policy position of strategic ambiguity regarding Israel’s weapons program. It is a strange game where everyone knows the truth but does not speak it out loud, leaving Israel’s status suspended in the air. It is thought that Israel has boosted fission nuclear weapons and potentially untested thermonuclear and neutron bomb designs based on research data from its collaborations with France and South Africa. Modern boosted fission weapons are an order of magnitude more powerful than the two comparatively simple and morally shocking 15-20 kiloton city killers that America detonated in Japan. To give a sense of proportion, while American nuclear arsenals have had bombs up to 25 megatons in the 1960s, our modern strategy focuses on a greater number of lower-yield weapons in the hundred kiloton range. For the most part, this strategy is more efficient at destroying a given area than a larger bomb of equivalent strength (though the big ones are still useful when used with inaccurate missiles). In order for a research program to develop reliable weapon designs, it is crucial to obtain accurate explosive test data. Despite U.S. denials, it is likely that Israel collected test data in partnership with South Africa; a part of a test sequence was observed in the 1979 VELA satellite incident when a break in the cloud cover revealed a tell-tale double flash over the Southern Indian Ocean. Seymour Hersh wrote there were three tests, and the one that was caught by VELA was a low-yield nuclear artillery shell according to multiple unnamed Israeli government sources in his 1991 book “The Samson Option.” (Hersh, p. 271) Said French nuclear physicist Francis Perrin, who participated in discussions about building the reactor, “We thought the Israeli bomb was aimed at the Americans…. Not to launch it against America but to say, ‘If you don’t want to help us in a critical situation, we will require you to help us. Otherwise we will use our bombs.'” (Hersh, p. 40). There is an unfortunate realist logic to Israel’s nuclear policy. Since the country is so small, it cannot absorb a ground invasion force the way Russia, for example, has been able to historically. Therefore, since it is nuclear-armed, Israel has implied it will use its nuclear weapons in a first strike against non-nuclear states should it fear for the life of the state. A nuclear attack in the region would slaughter innocent people in the hundreds of thousands, millions, or tens of millions in a horrific manner . Additionally, Israel is located in an energy-rich region with critical shipping lanes. Such an attack would likely target economic targets like oil fields across the Middle East, obliterate them, and contaminate them with radioactive fallout. Shipping lanes would be disrupted, with ports destroyed or even tight geographic features like the Suez Canal could be damaged. Firestorms started by nuclear explosions could smoke into the stratosphere , which would linger for some time. The reduced sunlight would degrade agricultural output over a wide area (an effect termed “nuclear autumn”), creating famines that could be even more deadly than direct war damage. This is the kind of power the Tel Aviv Reich wields. It helps explain why the international community has barely lifted a finger to help the Palestinian people in the midst of a genocide where one 2025 projection estimates 680,000 Palestinians may have already perished from all causes. In addition to all the direct sticks and carrots American diplomats have undoubtedly deployed behind closed doors, they can also appeal to reason: You wouldn’t want them to go nuclear, would you? Such a situation as outlined above would be much worse for the economy than the current self-induced crisis in the Strait of Hormuz. Therefore, one might think that American planners would attempt to mitigate the risk of nuclear war—and mitigate it they do. You can see this in their harsh and unrelenting treatment of Iran, where they constantly talk about preventing an Iranian nuclear weapon. While I don’t believe this is their only motivating factor, nor that their treatment is justifiable on a moral or legal basis, it is true that they routinely set back Iranian nuclear chemistry capabilities with varying degrees of effectiveness. Iran bears American aggression because they do not possess a nuclear weapon. During the Korean War, North Korea had about 20% of its population wiped out in the 1950s by American aggression and was constantly antagonized until they acquired a nuclear deterrent and now appear to be safe. By contrast, Libya surrendered its nuclear program, and its leader Gaddafi was sodomized with a bayonet after America secured the safety of a militant insurgency from the air. Three different countries contradicting American interests, three different nuclear statuses, three different outcomes. Iran has nuclear potential and is resisting; Libya surrendered and was defeated; the DPRK succeeded and is secure. That doesn’t mean acquiring a nuclear weapon is some unalloyed good. It defers one immediate state-wide risk for a potentially wide-area or world-wide one that gets bigger with each country that acquires them. Israel offers a mirror perspective to examine. They already possess nuclear weapons. If America treated Israel like we do Iran, such as by routinely assassinating their citizens and invading their airspace, Israel would probably perform a nuclear strike, so that approach is ruled out. If Iran treated Israel like America treats Iran, that too could trigger a nuclear launch. Hence, Iran is very careful about calibrating its actions and signaling its position in the escalation ladder when it does act. It’s not in America’s interest for Israel to wage nuclear war in a highly sensitive region. So how does America “contain” Israel? With flowers instead of swords, in what is frequently termed a “bear hug.” America provides a conventional security guarantee to avoid existential Israeli anxiety that stems from their extensive history of criminality and territorial vulnerability. The word “anxiety” is important because Israeli anxieties may become detached from reality, but America’s military commitment must scale with them lest they launch the nukes. After Operation Al-Aqsa Flood on October 7, 2023, the settler-colony’s paranoia has become all-consuming, attacking everyone and everything around it viciously and without conscience. The Israeli public’s blood lust gives Nazi Germany a run for its money—in 2024, 73% of the citizenry, amidst a horrific slaughter of children, thought that the job the military was doing was “about right” or “not far enough.” With Israel’s international reputation in tatters, and with Israel’s domestic politics stabilized by expansionary war, they are attempting to complete and solidify their conquests with all possible haste, hoping that all will be forgiven, or at least tolerated, in the gleaming light of victory. American military commitments have paced Israel’s expansionist aggression and genocidal revenge. In 1956, when the Dimona research facility was still in its early phases, Bertrand Goldschmidt, who was present at a meeting of the French Atomic Energy Commission, shared,: “…They [the Israeli delegation] said that when the Americans will realize we have a nuclear capacity, they will give us the guarantee of survival. All this was decided before the Suez Affair.” (p. 39) To put it crudely, Israel has America by the balls, and America is smiling. Lest you think this is an exaggeration, in the chapter “Nuclear Blackmail” of “The Samson Option,” during the 1973 Yom Kippur War Israel was losing badly, and their military was threatening to collapse for lack of supplies. Henry Kissinger was considering letting Egypt bleed Israel a bit and then have the two sides settle for peace on more balanced terms. Instead, the Israelis raised a nuclear alert and forced him into an immediate conventional arms resupply. In a second incident, during the first Gulf War, Hersh describes how in response to Iraqi truck-mounted Scud missiles that were rumored to be loaded with chemical weapons, Israel raised a nuclear alert that lasted for weeks and visibly pointed its nuclear launchers at Iraq. In response, America offered money, patriot missile batteries, and marked Scud launchers as priority targets. It turned out the Scuds were conventionally armed. (Hersh, p. 318) The attitude of John McCone, CIA Director in 1961, was reported by Walt Elder, an executive assistant to the CIA, as, “He thought an Israeli bomb would lead to escalation and then you could just cross off oil from the Middle East for years.” (Hersh, p. 106) In February 1968, just before Israel had completed its first bomb, according to Schlomo Aronson, Henry Kissinger said to a group of Israeli scholars that the United States would not “lift a finger” to help in case of a Soviet missile attack—right after Israeli intelligence learned that four Israeli cities had been added to Soviet nuclear targeting lists. (Hersh, p. 177) There is also a historical coincidence that occludes the nuclear aspect in some discussions of the America-Israeli relationship. Around the time Israel acquired its first nuclear weapons, the country also fought and won the Six-Day War. This was the moment Israel proved itself to America and the Zionist lobby started to become included in major decisions. Anti-semitism went from highly prevalent to a no-no. Due to this timing, aggressive containment of Israel’s nukes was never on the table (though there was substantial but ineffective pressure for IAEA inspections of the Negev Nuclear Research Facility). Thus, containment with flowers was born. All the incentives align—and while American planners inside think-tanks and the military may not have particularly wanted Israel to get a nuke (though they pointedly looked the other way according to Hersh), American Zionist businesspeople with close ties to the U.S. government helped finance Israel’s acquisition of nuclear technology from France. France agreed to sell Israel a nuclear reactor in exchange for help retaining French Algeria as well as due to mutual nuclear collaboration with scientists when France was building its own weapon. While sending conventional arms to Israel helps forestall imminent use, it is something of a band-aid. Israel is still a tiny state that is unable to absorb land invasions. This causes considerable existential anxiety. If Israel were territorially bigger, this anxiety would be reduced (and it would have more natural resources, making it more self-sustaining). Thus, there is at least one rational basis for at least some U.S. planners to support the “Greater Israel” project to take over the Middle East even though there is no possible legal or moral justification for this concept. Another dismal aspect to consider is that based on the disclosures by Mordecai Vanunu, Israel likely has advanced “clean” neutron weapons that have vastly reduced fallout compared to standard designs. (Hersh, p. 199-200) This has serious implications because it increases their willingness to use nuclear weapons in proximity to nearby population centers – such as Gaza. One shouldn’t assume that just because our government supports Israel and doesn’t publicly mention their nuclear capability doesn’t mean the military doesn’t make certain considerations for it. Despite my longstanding serious grievances with the U.S. military, I don’t think they would like other countries to be freelancing nuclear war. Therefore, the deployment of naval vessels and bases around Israel possibly has a dual purpose. If Israel plays along, we use those assets to protect their territory and reduce their existential dread. If they launch nuclear missiles, those assets can be used to try to shut down their remaining launch capability, and in certain lucky cases, perhaps shoot down an impulsive limited launch, particularly if there was forewarning. If that shut-down capability is used, the “special relationship” would be over, so if there are such plans, they would only be used as a last resort. Even if they are in place, I’m not confident that the realists would win the argument over the ideologues. According to Hersh, Israel has missiles, bomber aircraft, long-range nuclear artillery shells, suitcase nukes, and nuclear landmines—it is not possible to stop them if they are really determined to use their capability. containing nuclear apartheid How can the Israeli war machine and settler-colonial project be stopped? There are some unfortunate facts. The first is that no state will intervene militarily in Israel’s territory in a way that seriously scares them for fear of inciting a nuclear strike. Conventional missile attacks have a much more limited capacity to ignite that kind of fear—air power alone is generally insufficient to overthrow a government. Iran, Lebanon, and Yemen have launched missiles and rockets, but no military has dared to cross the border to assist the internal Palestinian Resistance since the first day of Operation Al-Aqsa Flood, when resistance fighters streamed out of Gaza. The focus has been instead on containing and punishing Israeli aggression in very measured ways. The safest strategy is to aid in causing the nuclear-armed apartheid state to collapse internally via economic sanctions. However, so long as nothing is done about the nukes, they can continue to get away with applying the Dahyia doctrine of total destruction wherever they attack. The unfortunate truth is that it would take decades for a tough sanctions regime to start to make a dent in their nuclear capability. One should not expect the apartheid regime to fall quietly. When the victory comes, it is plausible that, as in the South African case, the Israeli government would destroy their own nukes rather than hand them over to Palestinians as part of shared democratic governance. We can expect the revolutionaries to have to make hard and swift decisions to attempt to avoid the worst. In the United States, we will need to do our part to support the new Palestinian government. Speak the Truth about Israeli Nuclear Weapons Iran historically did not want a nuclear weapon, but given the current unprovoked assault on Iran and the reality of Israeli nuclear weapons, and with their biggest opponent, Ayatollah Khamenei, assassinated, they would be foolish not to consider acquiring a deterrent. In response to this situation of its own making, the U.S. is considering providing civil nuclear technology to Saudi Arabia , so if Iran were to acquire a deterrent, Saudi Arabia might not be too many years behind them. This is a nightmare of nuclear proliferation that could cause other countries at odds with these powers to become interested in their own capability. The risks to the region and the world would keep increasing. There could be some positives if Iran obtained nuclear capability. For example, they could extend their nuclear umbrella to Lebanon and Gaza, much as the U.S. does for NATO allies; this would do much for curbing Israeli excesses and would give the Palestinian resistance much-needed relief from the constant onslaught of the occupation forces. An Iranian deterrent would secure the safety of Iran from invasion, provide the Palestinians with a lifeline, and contain the Greater Israel project. It might even open the door to the fall of apartheid Israel. However, these positives would come at the risk of a two-sided nuclear war in the Middle East with all that entails—including the risk of entangling other nuclear powers. The root cause of this situation is Israel’s behavior, the fact of Israel’s nuclear arsenal, and the actions of the United States. This can all be avoided if Israel were to denuclearize, which will only be possible if the United States insists on it. What is our contribution? DSA can immediately help by talking about Israeli nukes officially and pointing out the difference in how Israel and Iran are treated on this issue. This will impede American aggression against Iran and give Iran a political lifeline. I suspect that some DSA congresspeople have been reluctant to speak on this issue because of the nuclear gag. For example, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has for years maintained a very controversial position of supporting defensive weapons such as interceptor missiles for the Israeli military but not offensive weapons like guns, tanks, bombs, etc. These defensive weapons, of course, allow the Israeli military to commit crimes without taking a hit back. Recently, in concert with the Israeli government signaling they’re okay with it , she has adopted the finely threaded position that defensive weapons are good, but Israel has to pay for them. It is hard to know what someone is truly thinking, but one very charitable explanation for AOC’s bizarre position is a credible fear of Israel starting a nuclear war. U.S. government officials have been reticent to talk about Israeli nukes for the entire duration of the program, even within the confines of the intelligence agencies. On March 26, 2026, Rep. Ilhan Omar was interviewed on the subject of Israeli nukes: “We’re able to talk about what kind of nukes we have. We have always been able to talk about the nukes that exist with our allies. The fact that we can’t have a discussion on Israel’s nukes, whether they have it or whether they tried to acquire it, and how much they have… it tells you that the level of fear that exists in Washington when it comes to questioning anything Israel and its army is doing.” On May 5th, she and thirty of her colleagues, led by Rep. Joaquin Castro, presented a letter to Sec. of State Marco Rubio demanding clarity on Israel’s nuclear capability in stark terms, yet still hedged their language in terms of possibilities rather than a frank acknowledgement. She came close, but Ms. Omar and her colleagues stopped short of recognizing a reality that has been evident for decades. She did not break the taboo. Nonetheless, there is momentum on this issue. Breaking the taboo will have impacts on the Non-Proliferation Treaty. It will rearrange nuclear policy in the Middle East. It will refocus attention on the real reason for the aggression against Iran: ensuring Israel retains nuclear supremacy over its neighbors. My fellow comrades in the DSA, it is important that we continue to raise the banner of Palestine every chance we get and build pressure to disarm Israel. It is clear that this is a central challenge of our time. We must be able to push boundaries. We must defend the humanity of Palestinians and support the fall of the apartheid state as quickly as possible. We must talk about denuclearizing Israel. reference Hersh, Seymour M. The Samson Option: Israel’s Nuclear Arsenal and American Foreign Policy . 1. ed., 2. print, Random House, 1991. ISBN 0-394-57006-5
